plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.4.5
plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates how constant-parameter lines in the uv-parameter domain map to curves on a parametric surface in 3D space. Left panel: the uv-plane showing a vertical orange line labeled u constant and a horizontal purple line labeled v constant. Right panel: a smooth curved parametric patch in xyz-space, with a constant u-curve highlighted in orange and a constant v-curve highlighted in purple on the surface; families of such curves form the curvilinear coordinate grid covering the surface. An arrow connects the two panels to indicate the mapping. The figure establishes that fixing one parameter in a parametric surface equation produces a curve on the surface, and that families of u-curves and v-curves together form the natural coordinate grid on a parametric surface.

elements: small uv-parameter domain panel (inset, upper-left of view): u-axis horizontal, v-axis vertical, thin frame over [-1.5,1.5]×[0,3]
vertical orange line in the uv panel marking the fixed u value, labeled 'u constant'
horizontal purple line in the uv panel marking the fixed v value, labeled 'v constant'
moving marker dot at the intersection of the two lines in the uv panel
3D xyz axes at the origin: x forward-left, y right, z up
grey parametric surface patch r(u,v) rendered from the current equations
faint grey curvilinear grid of constant-u and constant-v lines covering the surface
highlighted orange constant-u curve on the surface (v varies, u fixed)
highlighted purple constant-v curve on the surface (u varies, v fixed)
moving marker point on the surface at r(u,v) corresponding to the domain dot
labels: 'Constant u-curve' near the orange curve, 'Constant v-curve' near the purple curve

interactions.label: r(u,v) =
interactions.teaches: The algebraic form of r(u,v) fully determines the surface: editing any component reshapes the patch and bends the constant-u and constant-v curves with it, showing the parameter curves are intrinsic to the parametrization

interactions.label: u (fixed value for u-curve)
interactions.teaches: Fixing u while v runs free traces one constant-u curve on the surface; sweeping u slides that curve across the patch, showing the family of u-curves fills the surface

interactions.label: v (fixed value for v-curve)
interactions.teaches: Fixing v while u runs free traces one constant-v curve; sweeping v moves it across the surface, showing the two families together form a curvilinear coordinate grid
Rotating the view reveals the 3D shape of the surface and that the highlighted curves genuinely lie on it, not in a plane

demo_steps.title: Default cone
demo_steps.narration: The default r(u,v) = (u·cos v, u·sin v, u) is a cone. The orange vertical line u = const in the domain maps to the orange circle-like constant-u curve on the surface; the purple horizontal line v = const maps to the purple straight rulings (constant-v curve).

demo_steps.title: Sweep u
demo_steps.narration: Drag u from small to large: the orange u-curve slides up the cone and grows — circles of radius u at height z = u. The family of these curves covers the whole surface.

demo_steps.title: Sweep v
demo_steps.narration: Now sweep v: the purple v-curve rotates around the cone along a straight generator line. Together the two families form the curvilinear grid on the surface.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Default surface is the cone r(u,v) = (u cos v, u sin v, u) with u ∈ [0, 2], v ∈ [0, 2π]; apex at origin, opening upward to z = 2, rim radius 2. 3D axes: x axis ~2.5 long pointing forward-left, y ~2.5 pointing right, z ~2.5 up, black with arrowheads and italic labels x, y, z. Surface patch light grey #cccccc, slightly translucent (opacity ~0.85), smooth-shaded. Grid lines grey #666666, thin (~9 u-lines and 9 v-lines). Highlighted constant-u curve orange #e8862e, thick tube; highlighted constant-v curve purple #a0519e, thick tube. Marker point at r(u,v) small dark sphere. uv panel inset in the upper-left as a small flat 2D diagram: u-axis horizontal, v-axis vertical, domain rectangle u ∈ [0,2], v ∈ [0,2π] (normalized in display), vertical orange line at the slider u value labeled 'u constant', horizontal purple line at the slider v value labeled 'v constant', intersection dot. The orange and purple of the domain lines must exactly match the corresponding surface curves so the mapping is read off by color.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the surface as a ParametricGeometry-style BufferGeometry sampled ~60×60 over (u,v); rebuild on every equation edit (debounced), and on parse error show an inline message and keep the last valid surface. Recompute grid lines, the two highlighted curves, and the marker point reactively on slider changes without rebuilding the whole mesh (highlight curves are separate tube/line objects). Guard against NaN/Infinity from user equations by clamping or skipping bad sample rows. The uv panel can be an orthographic overlay or a billboarded plane that always faces the camera; its highlight lines update with the sliders. Keep equation input fields in a panel along the top or side so both the domain inset and the 3D view remain visible.

Left panel: the uv-plane showing a vertical orange line labeled u constant and a horizontal purple line labeled v constant. Right panel: a smooth curved parametric patch in xyz-space, with a constant u-curve highlighted in orange and a constant v-curve highlighted in purple on the surface; families of such curves form the curvilinear coordinate grid covering the surface. An arrow connects the two panels to indicate the mapping. The figure establishes that fixing one parameter in a parametric surface equation produces a curve on the surface, and that families of u-curves and v-curves together form the natural coordinate grid on a parametric surface.
authoredInteractions:
- equation input for the parametric surface: three fields for x(u,v), y(u,v), z(u,v) pre-filled with a simple example (e.g. x=u*cos(v), y=u*sin(v), z=u); when the learner edits any component the 3D surface redraws and the constant-u and constant-v grid curves update — shows how the algebraic form of r(u,v) determines the surface geometry and the shape of the parameter curves

authoredContext: We have seen that curves in 3-space can be represented by three equations involving one parameter, say x = x(t), y = y(t), z = z(t) Surfaces in 3-space can be represented parametrically by three equations involving two parameters, say x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v), z = z(u, v) (3) To visualize why such equations represent a surface, think of (u, v) as a point that varies over some region in a uv-plane. If u is held constant, then v is the only varying parameter in (3), and hence these equations represent a curve in 3-space. We call this a constant u-curve (Figure 14.4.5). Similarly, if v is held constant, then u is the only varying parameter in (3), so again these equations represent a curve in 3-space. We call this a constant v-curve. By varying the constants we generate a family of u-curves and a family of v-curves that together form a surface.

demo_steps.narration: Now sweep v: the purple v-curve rotates around the cone along a straight generator line. Together the two families form the curvilinear grid on the surface.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Default surface is the cone r(u,v) = (u cos v, u sin v, u) with u ∈ [0, 2], v ∈ [0, 2π]; apex at origin, opening upward to z = 2, rim radius 2. 3D axes: x axis ~2.5 long pointing forward-left, y ~2.5 pointing right, z ~2.5 up, black with arrowheads and italic labels x, y, z. Surface patch light grey #cccccc, slightly translucent (opacity ~0.85), smooth-shaded. Grid lines grey #666666, thin (~9 u-lines and 9 v-lines). Highlighted constant-u curve orange #e8862e, thick tube; highlighted constant-v curve purple #a0519e, thick tube. Marker point at r(u,v) small dark sphere. uv panel inset in the upper-left as a small flat 2D diagram: u-axis horizontal, v-axis vertical, domain rectangle u ∈ [0,2], v ∈ [0,2π] (normalized in display), vertical orange line at the slider u value labeled 'u constant', horizontal purple line at the slider v value labeled 'v constant', intersection dot. The orange and purple of the domain lines must exactly match the corresponding surface curves so the mapping is read off by color.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the surface as a ParametricGeometry-style BufferGeometry sampled ~60×60 over (u,v); rebuild on every equation edit (debounced), and on parse error show an inline message and keep the last valid surface. Recompute grid lines, the two highlighted curves, and the marker point reactively on slider changes without rebuilding the whole mesh (highlight curves are separate tube/line objects). Guard against NaN/Infinity from user equations by clamping or skipping bad sample rows. The uv panel can be an orthographic overlay or a billboarded plane that always faces the camera; its highlight lines update with the sliders. Keep equation input fields in a panel along the top or side so both the domain inset and the 3D view remain visible.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates how constant-parameter lines in the uv-parameter domain map to curves on a parametric surface in 3D space. Left panel: the uv-plane showing a vertical orange line labeled u constant and a horizontal purple line labeled v constant. Right panel: a smooth curved parametric patch in xyz-space, with a constant u-curve highlighted in orange and a constant v-curve highlighted in purple on the surface; families of such curves form the curvilinear coordinate grid covering the surface. An arrow connects the two panels to indicate the mapping. The figure establishes that fixing one parameter in a parametric surface equation produces a curve on the surface, and that families of u-curves and v-curves together form the natural coordinate grid on a parametric surface.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- equation input for the parametric surface: three fields for x(u,v), y(u,v), z(u,v) pre-filled with a simple example (e.g. x=u*cos(v), y=u*sin(v), z=u); when the learner edits any component the 3D surface redraws and the constant-u and constant-v grid curves update — shows how the algebraic form of r(u,v) determines the surface geometry and the shape of the parameter curves
- sliders for u and v: sweep the highlighted constant-u (orange) and constant-v (pink) curves across the surface
plan.sourcePath: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.4.5
